I’ve loved the song for many years, after I heard Dave Fanning (a magnificent DJ on Irish radio) play it late one night when I was a teenager in search of music. So: the letter. recent_candidates.title: Tanzania and Angola reach agreement to connect rail corridors
recent_candidates.author: Tiisetso Motsoeneng
recent_candidates.excerpt: Tanzania and Angola have agreed to connect railways serving ports on opposite coasts of Africa, Tanzania’s president said. The move brings together multibillion-dollar infrastructure backed by Western governments and China. The proposed connection of the Western-backed Lobito Corridor with China-backed TAZARA would stretch between ports on Angola’s Atlantic coast and Tanzania’s Indian Ocean coast through Zambia and DR Congo, home to Africa’s richest deposits of copper and cobalt — minerals deemed vital to economic security amid the global energy transition. The agreement complicates the geopolitical narrative around both railways because connecting them would turn rival corridors into a coast-to-coast network, putting Zambia and Congo in a position where they have access to both oceans without having to choose between China and the West. The plan may be seen as illustrating an argument that developing countries are resisting pressure to choose camps in the growing competition between Washington and Beijing. The agreement comes days after the Africa Finance Corporation picked contractors for sections of the new Zambia-Lobito railway. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

recent_candidates.title: Uganda calls for AU force to contain Ebola outbreak
recent_candidates.author: Ruben Nyanguila
recent_candidates.excerpt: Uganda has called on the African Union to consider deploying its standby peacekeeping and humanitarian force to help contain an Ebola outbreak that has killed nearly 5,000 people in DR Congo. The call was made at a meeting of health officials from 45 African countries who came together to coordinate a continent-wide response to the outbreak, which has infected more than 10,000 people in DR Congo and now spread to Kenya and Nigeria. Uganda’s health minister told the summit on Wednesday that AU personnel could provide medical and logistical support, and help ease a shortage of health workers. He called on leaders to hold an emergency meeting to decide on financing and deployment. Officials agreed to strengthen cross-border surveillance, share information, and keep borders open. The virus has now spread further across Africa than any previous Ebola outbreak, with cases in the continent’s central, eastern, and western regions. — Ruben Nyanguila

recent_candidates.title: Lagos Fashion Week returns with focus on sustainability
recent_candidates.author: Yinka Adegoke
recent_candidates.excerpt: Lagos Fashion Week returned for its 15th edition this week, bringing together some of the continent’s best-known designers, including Lisa Folawiyo, Nkwo, Orange Culture, and Emmy Kasbit. But the event is increasingly about more than runway recognition: This year’s theme, “Crafted,” puts heritage, craftsmanship, and circular fashion at the center, say the organizers, and reflects Lagos Fashion Week’s growing emphasis on building a commercially viable and sustainable African fashion industry. The ambition is to turn global interest in African design into lasting economic opportunities for local manufacturers, artisans, and creative businesses. “African fashion doesn’t have a creativity problem, it has an infrastructure problem,” Omoyemi Akerele, founder of Lagos Fashion Week, told Semafor. “Access to finance, manufacturing capacity, and distribution remain significant barriers.” — Yinka Adegoke

recent_candidates.title: Africa Cup of Nations U-turn on four-year cycle
recent_candidates.author: Alexander Onukwue
recent_candidates.excerpt: The Africa Cup of Nations, the continent’s top football competition, will continue to be held biennially, reversing a plan to introduce a four-year cycle put forward by the Confederation of African Football. Announcing the U-turn, CAF placed financial considerations at the heart of its reasoning. Patrice Motsepe, the South African billionaire who runs CAF and championed the shift, said the reversal was in the interest of the organization’s 54 member nations and African players who ply their trade abroad. AFCON games have risen in global recognition over recent editions, expanding revenue streams for CAF. recent_candidates.title: South African lender Absa opens Gulf office
recent_candidates.author: Tiisetso Motsoeneng
recent_candidates.excerpt: South Africa’s third-largest lender, Absa, opened its first Gulf office, giving the bank a seat closer to Middle Eastern investors hunting for deals on the continent. Absa joins South African rivals Standard Bank, Nedbank, and Investec, which have already established a presence in Dubai. Absa CEO Kenny Fihla said the office, which is looking to benefit from advisory and credit-arrangement fees, would help “connect capital from the region and from wider international markets with opportunities across Africa.” Gulf-backed ports, logistics, and energy projects are expanding along Africa’s eastern seaboard. The trend has incentivized continental banks to double down on East Africa and strengthen links with the Gulf. Capital from that region has become more visible across the continent: Gulf Cooperation Council countries have pumped more than $100 billion into Africa over the past decade. The United Arab Emirates is now Africa’s fourth-largest foreign investor behind China, the EU, and the US. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

recent_candidates.title: Oman stands out amongst Gulf markets weathering disruption
recent_candidates.author: Kelsey Warner
recent_candidates.excerpt: Oman is the standout among Gulf stock markets that have otherwise struggled this year. Still, as elsewhere, markets are not the economy: The IMF has forecast a 4.8% contraction in the Gulf’s GDP in 2026, but stocks haven’t plunged as much, suggesting stronger-than-expected corporate earnings have supported valuations. Within the relatively thin universe of equities, one name outshines all: Saudi Aramco accounted for about 72% of the combined earnings of Tadawul-listed companies in the first half of the year. Higher crude prices lifted its net profit 33%, and with oil up since Houthi attacks intensified on the kingdom, Aramco may have another strong quarter when it announces its results on Nov. 3. — Kelsey Warner

recent_candidates.title: Oracle among AI firms forging ahead with Gulf expansion
recent_candidates.author: Kelsey Warner
recent_candidates.excerpt: US artificial intelligence firms are expanding in the Gulf, a sign that some companies are not shying away despite increased risks to digital infrastructure. Oracle plans to build more data centers in Saudi Arabia and the UAE to meet rising demand, The National reported. And Scale AI, which is 49% owned by Meta and sells labeled data for model training, opened an office at the Dubai International Financial Center, following an agreement to work with a G42 unit to develop AI agents. In Saudi Arabia, New York-listed Snowflake projects it will invest $300 million in the kingdom through 2030; its customers there include dairy company Almarai and PIF-backed developer Red Sea Global. Led by former Google Ads chief Sridhar Ramaswamy, it has plans for two more cloud computing regions and, with the communications ministry, AI training for thousands of Saudis. So far, data center construction has “ barely moved the needle for Gulf economies,” according to Bloomberg economist Ziad Daoud. The Iran war makes building that infrastructure pricier and riskier; he wrote that hardened security adds 5% to 7% to costs. Still, it appears there is willingness to absorb the new premium. — Kelsey Warner

recent_candidates.title: Prediction markets flop on recent elections
recent_candidates.author: Liz Hoffman
recent_candidates.excerpt: Prediction markets blew three big elections this week, a bad look for platforms pitching themselves to investors as hedges against global risk. Kalshi and Polymarket both gave Brazilian conservative Flávio Bolsonaro a 4-in-5 chance of winning; he lost to the progressive incumbent, costing anyone who traded Brazil’s currency and stocks. The markets also overrated Netanyahu’s challenger in Israel, where the race is still too close to call — and where a series of suspicious bets elicited an investigation by Polymarket. In Serbia (emerging-market investors need good information, too!), Kalshi gave the heavily favored incumbent strongman 75% odds as late as election day. He lost. Kalshi has touted the accuracy of its markets to win over institutional investors. A hedge that doesn’t work is doubly bad: useless expensive. — Liz Hoffman

recent_candidates.title: Microsoft reaps the benefits of protecting its AAA credit rating
recent_candidates.author: Ellen DiMauro
recent_candidates.excerpt: Microsoft has protected its AAA credit rating — one of just two left in Corporate America, alongside Johnson & Johnson’s — and is reaping the rewards for its financial discipline. Despite the spreading fears about AI-related debt, the company raised $25 billion Thursday in its first bond offering since 2017. The deal’s 10-year portion cost just 5.6%, barely more than the US government pays to borrow. Further down the ratings ladder, investors are getting choosier and demanding higher yields to take on the risk of lending to companies in the AI sector. SpaceX, rated three rungs lower than Microsoft at BBB, will pay as much as 8.75% for its $40 billion haul this week, and neocloud CoreWeave’s bonds, deep in junk-rated territory, have traded at yields above 15%. In the race to bankroll the AI boom, the bond market is drawing a stark dividing line between borrowing at a bargain and paying a punishing premium. — Ellen DiMauro

Last week, AI firm Hirundo released a case study detailing its experiments with the open-weight Qwen3-Coder model from Chinese firm Alibaba. Hirundo prompted Qwen3-Coder to build a secrets storage app for different hypothetical customers and compared how secure the agent’s code was. The code's security was then benchmarked against BaxBench . In test cases, Qwen was variably told it was for working for a U.S. defense contractor, a Hong Kong democracy advocacy group, or a Chinese defense contractor. recent_candidates.author: Tahir Azad
recent_candidates.excerpt: The phrase “civilian nuclear program” implies a clean line: reactors that generate electricity, isotopes for medicine, and research neutrons on one side, and the enrichment plants and plutonium reactors that feed a weapons stockpile on the other. Across most of the world, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) polices that line through comprehensive safeguards. In South Asia, the line barely exists. India and Pakistan both operate power reactors under IAEA inspection while running weapons complexes a short distance away, drawing on shared expertise, shared institutions, and, in important respects, a shared fuel cycle. The “civilian” label survives less as a technical description than as a diplomatic and commercial instrument. Asking how civil these programs are exposes how porous the boundary is and why that porousness matters for the wider non-proliferation order. The ambiguity is not a recent complication; it is foundational. India’s first nuclear detonation in 1974 was carried out with plutonium produced in the Canadian-supplied CIRUS reactor, material provided on the understanding that it would be used only for peaceful purposes . New Delhi described the test as a “peaceful nuclear explosion,” a phrase that captured, perhaps unintentionally, just how indistinct the civil and military categories already were. recent_candidates.excerpt: “What will happen to the body?” I asked. “Oh, it will go out with the medical waste, it won’t be recognizable as a body,” said the doctor. “Do you have any other questions?” “Oh. I muddled my way through the rest of the appointment and then stopped at the desk to schedule my D&C for two days later. It was only Wednesday, but that week already had felt like eternity since the appointment on Monday when we learned our baby’s heartbeat had stopped. No matter what I did that week to process the grief, I felt like a walking tomb. It wasn’t until the D&C was over that I rested—the morning sickness stopped, the waiting stopped, the finality brought peace. But the weight of death lingered. Now, twelve years, two more miscarriages, and two live births later it is not the D&C I regret; it is my own shame at that single question that haunts me. This was the most important question I asked all week, or maybe ever: what will happen to my baby’s body? What will happen to my baby’s body? We never had the opportunity to dignify our miscarried babies through a Christian burial. We did what we could through private memorials, intentional prayers, and symbolic remembrances to mark their lives with solemn honor. We celebrated their entry into eternity with the Father, and we rested in their union with the Son.

recent_candidates.excerpt: El déficit público de España mantiene su imparable escalada.
